title: GraphQL Security Field Notes: From Resolver AuthZ to Persisted Queries
summary: A 10-page dense study-notes series on hardening GraphQL APIs: resolver and object-level authorization, introspection control, depth and cost limits, and persisted queries — with internals, comparisons, real pitfalls and a ship-it checklist.

chapters.title: Why GraphQL Breaks the Old Security Rules
points: Single endpoint: every operation arrives as one POST — URL-based firewalls and per-route ACLs cannot see intent.
Client-controlled shape: the query picks the fields, so over-fetching is attacker-chosen — scraping gets exactly the fields it wants.
The type system is the real attack surface: every type, field and argument added needs its own authorization decision.
AuthN vs authZ: authentication (who you are) usually runs before resolvers; authorization (what you may touch) must run inside them.
Introspection meta-fields (__schema, __type) hand attackers the full API map in one query — free reconnaissance.
Nesting + aliases: one document can trigger thousands of resolver calls (hero{friends{friends{...}}} with alias duplication) — a built-in DoS primitive.
GraphQL is not insecure by design; it moved control from routes to the graph, so your controls must move too.
OWASP API Top 10 maps fully: BOLA/IDOR, broken auth, unrestricted resource consumption all apply.
Arguments are attacker input: every ID, limit and filter in args needs validation like any REST parameter.
Errors are surface too: verbose errors leak schema hints, stack traces and object-existence info.
Baseline hardening order: authenticate → per-field authZ → cap size/depth/cost → gate introspection → persisted queries → monitor.
Rule zero: deny by default — a field with no explicit authorization decision is a leak waiting to be found.

chapters.title: Authorization in Resolvers: The Mechanics
points: Resolver signature (parent, args, context, info): authorization reads context.user — never trust args alone.
AuthN before execution: verify JWT/session in the server context function and attach user + roles so every resolver can check.
Deny-by-default pattern: a requireAuth/requireRole wrapper that throws ForbiddenError before any data access.
Field-level authZ: wrap individual resolvers when sensitivity varies inside one type (User.email vs User.name).
Type-level checks: guard whole types (e.g., AdminReport) with middleware that intercepts all of its resolvers.
Schema directives: @auth(requires: ADMIN) declared in SDL and enforced by a transform pass — policy lives next to the contract.
Rule libraries: GraphQL Shield builds a rule tree with per-rule caching; caveat — it only protects resolver entry points.
Minimum code to memorize: if (!ctx.user) throw new ForbiddenError() — then verify ownership of the specific object.
Object-level authZ belongs in the business/data layer when the decision needs the fetched object, not just the field name.
Subscriptions: authorize at connection setup AND again on each pushed event — a live channel outlives the original check.
Batching pitfall: DataLoader may serve cached records to users who could not fetch them — scope cache keys by user.
Response hygiene: throwing kills the whole document; returning null + an errors array masks just that field — choose deliberately.

chapters.title: Object-Level AuthZ & BOLA/IDOR
points: BOLA/IDOR defined: user A requests object(id: B's id) and gets it because the resolver only checked 'is logged in'.
It is the #1 OWASP API risk — GraphQL makes it trivial since every object is addressable through arguments.
Field checks do not cascade: securing Query.post does not protect post.author or post.comments — each type needs rules.
Ownership check pattern: fetch object → assert object.ownerId === ctx.user.id → else throw; cheap and explicit.
Better: scope the data source — WHERE owner_id = $user in SQL/Prisma so unauthorized rows are never fetched at all.
Postgres Row-Level Security: set the user id on the connection (set_config) and let the database enforce tenant isolation — defense in depth.
Centralize decisions as can(user, action, object) in a policy layer (CASL, Oso, custom) so rules do not scatter across 50 resolvers.
RBAC is coarse (roles), ABAC is contextual (owner, state, tenant) — most real APIs need both combined.
Existence leaks: 'forbidden' confirms the object exists; returning 'not found' hides it — pick per threat model.
Test adversarially: automated suite where user A requests every ID belonging to user B; run in CI on every schema change.
Log every denied access with user id + resource id — spikes signal scraping or probing.
Watch mutations too: updatePost(id:) with no ownership check is BOLA with write access — worse than a read.

chapters.title: Introspection: Reconnaissance & Control
points: __schema{types{...}} returns every type, field, argument, description and deprecation reason — a complete API blueprint.
Why attackers love it: instant discovery of admin mutations, internal types and still-live deprecated fields.
Turn it off in prod: Apollo Server introspection:false, GraphQL Yoga config flag, Graphene disable_introspection.
Naive blockers get bypassed: GET requests, multipart smuggling and extension tricks have snuck __schema past regex filters — test the real endpoint.
Field suggestions leak too: 'Did you mean secrets?' validates guesses — disable suggestion lists in prod.
Clairvoyance-style tools reconstruct schemas from suggestion leaks even with introspection 'disabled'.
Introspection is not a vulnerability itself — it is an information multiplier for authZ gaps and forgotten fields.
Cost of disabling: breaks GraphiQL, codegen and internal tooling — solve with environments, not by leaving it open.
Adaptive pattern: gate introspection on an auth header, admin role or internal network instead of a hard global off.
Schema registry alternative: publish SDL to an internal registry so teams keep tooling without runtime introspection.
Descriptions can leak: TODO notes and internal hostnames in field descriptions ship through introspection — audit them.
Verify, do not assume: run an actual __schema query after deploy and confirm the rejection shape.

chapters.title: Query Depth Limits
points: The attack: deeply nested selections (user→friends→friends→...) make resolver calls grow multiplicatively across levels.
Depth = the longest chain of fields from root to leaf; fragments count where they are spread.
Standard tool: the graphql-depth-limit validation rule — depthLimit(10) rejects documents past the cap before execution.
Calibrate to your schema: find the deepest legitimate operation (profile→orders→items→product) and set the limit just above it.
Aliases repeat subtrees within one document — depth counting must cover aliased branches, not only unique paths.
Know your library's semantics: how skip/include, fragments and interfaces are counted differs between implementations.
Depth is structural only: a shallow query with 500 aliased expensive fields sails past a depth cap — that is cost analysis' job.
Reject with a clean GraphQL validation error (fast, pre-execution) — never a 500 with a stack trace.
Cheap first line: cap document byte length (e.g., 2–10 KB) before parsing — kills the giant-document vector instantly.
Managed platforms differ: Hasura has native depth limits; AWS AppSync does not — approximate with WAF rules or pipeline resolvers.
Pair with execution timeouts and resolver invocation budgets so one unexpectedly slow field cannot hang the server.
Log rejected deep queries — legit clients tripping the limit means the cap is wrong, not the client.

chapters.title: Query Cost & Complexity Analysis
points: Idea: give each field a weight, multiply by list multipliers, sum the document, reject anything over budget before executing.
Multipliers make pagination sane: friends(first: 100) costs 100 × field weight — attackers cannot hide scale.
Compute cost after variable substitution: a static check on {first: $n} misses the attacker setting n = 100000.
Tools: graphql-cost-analysis (per-field costs in SDL), graphql-validation-complexity, Apollo's query complexity plugin.
Calibrate weights from reality: profile resolver latency — a 40 ms search field earns a far higher weight than a scalar.
Budgeting: start around 1000 points, log every rejection, and tune — rejected power-queries are your calibration data.
Cost vs depth: cost models volume and expensive fields; depth models nesting — they catch different attacks, use both.
Fragments must be expanded before scoring, or attackers hide costs inside named fragments.
Reject at the validation phase: the attacker pays parse cost only — no resolver execution, no database hits.
Rate-limit by cost, not request count: a token bucket where each request spends its computed cost — heavy queries drain it faster.
Reactive safety nets that still work: execution timeout plus a max-resolvers-per-query cap for anything your model missed.
Do not echo remaining budget in errors or extensions — fine-grained feedback helps attackers tune just under the cap.

chapters.title: Persisted Queries
points: Definition: operations are stored server-side by hash; the client sends only extensions.persistedQuery {version, sha256Hash} + variables.
APQ flow (Apollo): send hash → PersistedQueryNotFound → resend full document → server caches hash→document → hash only thereafter.
Hardened mode: whitelist-only — the server accepts only hashes present in the deployed manifest; unknown hashes are rejected.
Security payoff: attackers cannot invent new queries at all — depth/cost bypass attempts die at the door.
Manual persisted queries: generate the manifest at build time from frontend code and deploy it with the server — versions move together.
APQ vs manifest: APQ is convenient but registers whatever the client sends first; a manifest is strict but needs CI/CD discipline.
Client support: Apollo's persistedQueryLink, Relay (compiled queries by design), urql persisted-query exchanges.
Bonus: smaller payloads and no query text in URLs or logs — less sensitive information leaves the client.
Rollback discipline: keep old hashes alive until every shipped client version has migrated, or old apps break.
CI contract test: fail the build if any operation the shipped app uses is missing from the manifest.
Public-API fallback where you cannot whitelist: APQ + cost limits + depth limits + auth still beats nothing.
Cache safety: a hash is derived from the document content, so the hash→document mapping is immutable and cannot be poisoned.

chapters.title: Comparing Controls: Defense in Depth
points: Control matrix: token authN = who; resolver authZ = what data; introspection gating = recon; depth/cost = resource abuse; persisted queries = arbitrary ops.
Depth vs cost shapes: deep-narrow queries fail depth but pass cost; wide-shallow queries with expensive fields fail cost but pass depth.
Whitelist vs budget: persisted queries forbid everything unknown; cost limits allow anything within budget — first-party apps favor whitelists, public APIs favor budgets.
REST mapping: per-route rate limits and scoped tokens map roughly to per-operation cost limits; REST's fixed URLs make authz audits easy — GraphQL needs field-level rules instead.
Evaluation order: authenticate → parse → byte-size cap → whitelist check → depth → cost → resolvers with authZ.
Batching is a bypass: 50 cheap operations in one batch equals one expensive request — cap batch size and sum costs across it.
WAF reality: generic WAFs see one opaque POST — use GraphQL-aware rules (Cloudflare/AWS WAF) for depth and token counting, never as the only layer.
Fail closed on the whitelist (unknown = reject), fail monitored on cost heuristics (log + tune) — a buggy validator should not take the API down.
Stack rate limits: per-IP (coarse), per-user (fair), per-operation-cost (precise).
Observability: log operation name/hash, computed cost, user id and rejection flag; alert on new hashes once whitelisting.
Tooling conflict: introspection off means codegen needs a registry — plan the registry before flipping the flag.
Principle: every layer is bypassable alone; stacked layers raise attacker effort exponentially.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Real Gotchas
points: 'We have JWTs, we are safe' — authentication is not authorization; a logged-in user scraping others' data passes authN perfectly.
AuthZ on queries only: the deletePost mutation shipped with no ownership check — mutations need the same or stricter rules.
Depth limit left at a library default like 100 — that equals no limit; set it to your schema's real maximum plus margin.
Introspection disabled on the public domain but left on and reachable on staging/preview deployments.
Cost analysis trusted without variable clamping: first: 999999 turned a cheap-looking query into a table scan.
APQ deployed in 'allow any query' fallback mode in prod — zero whitelist benefit, all of the complexity paid.
Regex introspection blocker bypassed via GET or multipart smuggling — always verify with real adversarial tools.
DataLoader cache shared across users served one tenant another tenant's records — scope cache keys by user.
GraphQL over GET enabled with a cookie session = CSRF-able state changes; require POST plus SameSite/CSRF tokens.
Verbose prod errors leaked stack traces and resolver paths — disable stack traces and mask internal errors.
A shared API key extracted from the mobile app let attackers hit the API directly — pin certificates, whitelist queries, watch anomalies.
Meta-mistake: merging new fields without an authZ review — new schema surface is new attack surface; require a security check in schema PRs.

chapters.title: Hardening Cheat Sheet — Ship It
points: Order of operations: authN at context → deny-by-default authZ per field/object → size cap → depth → cost → whitelist → execute.
AuthZ minimum: every sensitive field has an explicit rule; prefer ownership-scoped data queries over post-fetch filtering.
Introspection: off or role-gated in prod, field suggestions off, SDL distributed via an internal registry, descriptions audited.
Depth limit: set from your schema's deepest legitimate query (commonly 7–12); reject with a validation error.
Cost limit: weights × pagination multipliers computed after variables; start near 1000 points and tune with rejection logs.
Persisted queries: CI-generated manifest for first-party apps; APQ + limits as the public-API fallback; keep old hashes through rollouts.
Also cap: batch size, document bytes, execution timeout, resolver invocations per query.
Monitoring: log cost, hash, user and rejections; alert on novel query shapes and spikes of denied authorization.
Testing: adversarial BOLA suite, introspection-bypass probes, and oversized/deep query fixtures running in CI.
Three questions for every new field: who can read this, who can write this, and what would an attacker do with it?
Posture scales with attacker cost: each stacked control multiplies their effort while a registry and docs keep developer velocity.
